bank.why: Metformin lowers liver glucose output without forcing insulin release.

bank.q: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors lower fasting blood glucose.
bank.why: They only blunt post-meal spikes; they have no effect on fasting glucose.

bank.q: Sitagliptin causes weight loss.
bank.why: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral; GLP-1 agonists cause weight loss.

bank.q: Blood pressure equals...
bank.why: BP = CO × SVR, and CO = HR × SV. Every antihypertensive lowers one of these (or the blood volume behind CO).

bank.q: Cardiac output equals...
bank.why: CO = HR × SV.

bank.q: Systolic blood pressure is the pressure in the arteries...
d: When the heart is relaxed between beats
bank.why: Systolic = upper number, during contraction (at the heartbeat); diastolic = lower number, heart relaxed.

bank.q: In a reading of 150/90, the 90 is the...
bank.a: Diastolic pressure, while the heart is relaxed
d: Systolic pressure, while the heart contracts
bank.why: Lower number = diastolic, between beats.

bank.q: Which INCREASES systemic vascular resistance?
bank.why: SVR rises with higher viscosity (polycythemia), longer total vessel length (obesity) and smaller radius (vasoconstriction).

bank.q: Polycythemia raises blood pressure mainly by increasing...
bank.why: More RBCs → thicker blood → more resistance.

bank.q: Obesity raises SVR mainly by increasing...
bank.why: A bigger body needs more vessels → longer total length → more resistance.

bank.q: Which raises heart rate?
bank.a: Increased sympathetic impulses and adrenal medulla hormones
bank.why: ↓ parasympathetic or ↑ sympathetic (and adrenal epinephrine) → ↑ HR → ↑ CO.

bank.q: Which does NOT increase venous return?
bank.why: Venous return rises with blood volume, the muscle and respiratory pumps, and VENOconstriction.
bank.hint: Which one pools blood in the veins?

bank.q: Which hormone LOWERS blood pressure?
bank.why: ANP vasodilates and lowers blood volume. Angiotensin II, aldosterone and ADH all raise BP.

bank.q: Which hormone raises BP by increasing blood volume?
bank.why: Blood volume ↑: aldosterone, ADH. Blood volume ↓: ANP.

bank.q: Which substance lowers BP by vasodilation?
bank.why: Vasodilators in Table 21.2: ANP, epinephrine (β2), nitric oxide.

bank.q: Epinephrine dilates the arterioles of skeletal and cardiac muscle through...
bank.why: Table footnote: epinephrine acts at β2 in cardiac and skeletal muscle arterioles; at α1 elsewhere it constricts.

bank.q: Which is NOT one of the four anatomic sites of blood pressure control?
bank.why: Four sites: arterioles (resistance), venules (capacitance), heart (pump output), kidneys (volume).

bank.q: Which vessels are the RESISTANCE vessels in BP control?
bank.why: Arterioles = resistance; venules = capacitance.

bank.q: Which vessels are the CAPACITANCE vessels?
bank.why: Venules hold (store) blood = capacitance.

bank.q: The kidneys control blood pressure mainly through...
bank.a: Blood volume, via renin → angiotensin → aldosterone
bank.why: Site 4: kidneys = volume control (RAAS).

bank.q: Hypertension is diagnosed based on...
bank.a: Repeated, reproducible measurements of elevated BP
d: One high reading in the clinic
bank.why: Slides: repeated, reproducible measurements.

bank.q: Hypertension with no specific cause is called...
bank.why: Primary (essential) = no specific cause; secondary = specific etiology.

bank.q: Hypertension caused by a pheochromocytoma is...
bank.why: It has a specific etiology, so it's secondary.

bank.q: Sophia's repeated readings average 125/78 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Elevated = 120–129 AND below 80.

bank.q: Abdel's repeated readings average 135/85 mmHg. How is this classified?
A patient's readings average 125/85 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Elevated needs systolic 120–129 AND diastolic < 80. A diastolic of 85 is in the 80–89 range, and stage 1 needs only one number (OR).

bank.q: A young man's readings average 118/92 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Stage 2 = ≥140 OR ≥90. A diastolic of 92 alone makes it stage 2.

bank.q: A patient's BP is 190/110 mmHg. How is this classified?
bank.why: Crisis = above 180 and/or above 120. Systolic 190 qualifies.

bank.q: Repeated readings of 150/95 mmHg are classified as...
bank.why: Stage 2 = ≥140 or ≥90.

bank.q: Repeated readings of 119/79 mmHg are classified as...
bank.why: Normal = below 120 AND below 80.

bank.q: To be classified as "Elevated", BOTH the systolic must be 120–129 AND the diastolic below 80.
bank.why: Normal and Elevated use AND; stages 1 and 2 use OR (either number).

bank.q: Diuretics lower blood pressure mainly by...
d: Blocking β1 receptors in the heart
bank.why: Slides: diuretics lower BP by depleting body sodium stores.

bank.q: In most patients, diuretics lower BP by about...
bank.why: Slides: 10–15 mmHg; used alone in mild or moderate essential hypertension.

bank.q: Diuretics may be used ALONE in...
bank.why: Slides: used alone in mild or moderate essential hypertension.

bank.q: Acetazolamide acts at the...
bank.why: Sites in nephron order: acetazolamide (PCT), osmotic (PCT + descending limb), loop (TAL), thiazide (DCT), K-sparing (collecting duct). A-O-L-T-K.

bank.q: Acetazolamide is a...
bank.why: Acetazolamide = carbonic anhydrase inhibitor at the PCT.

bank.q: Which is an osmotic diuretic?
bank.why: Mannitol (osmotic) acts at the PCT and descending limb.

bank.q: Which diuretic acts on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?
bank.why: Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid) act in the TAL.

bank.q: Which diuretic acts on the distal convoluted tubule?
bank.why: Thiazides (HCTZ, chlorthalidone, metolazone) block NCC in the DCT.
bank.hint: T for thiazide, T for disTal.

bank.q: Which diuretic acts in the collecting duct?
bank.why: K-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, triamterene) act in the collecting tubule/duct.

bank.q: Which drug inhibits NKCC2, the Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransporter?
bank.why: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the TAL. Metolazone = thiazide-like (NCC), eplerenone and triamterene = K-sparing.

bank.q: Which drug blocks the Na+/Cl− cotransporter (NCC) in the DCT?
bank.why: Thiazides and thiazide-like drugs (chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone) block NCC.

bank.q: Which drug blocks the epithelial Na+ channel (ENaC)?
bank.why: ENaC inhibitors: amiloride, triamterene. Spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor instead.

bank.q: Which drug blocks the aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor?
bank.why: Aldosterone antagonists: spironolactone, eplerenone.

bank.q: The two PROTOTYPE loop diuretics on the slide are...
bank.why: Slide: 2 prototype drugs, furosemide and ethacrynic acid; bumetanide and torsemide are the others.

bank.q: Steve has acute pulmonary edema: severe breathlessness and crackles in both lungs. Which diuretic is used?
bank.why: Loop diuretics: acute pulmonary edema and other edematous conditions (the strongest diuretics).

bank.q: A patient's serum K+ is dangerously high. Which diuretic helps remove K+?
bank.why: Loop diuretics are used for hyperkalemia (they waste K+). K-sparing diuretics would raise K+ further.

bank.q: Which is NOT a listed use of loop diuretics?
bank.why: Loop uses: pulmonary edema/edema, hyperkalemia, acute renal failure. Hyperaldosteronism is a K-sparing (spironolactone) use.

bank.q: A patient on IV diuretics for heart failure complains of ringing in the ears and hearing loss. Which drug?
bank.why: Loop diuretic toxicity: ototoxicity and allergic reactions. The ear has a loop too.

bank.q: The usual total daily oral dose of furosemide is...
bank.why: Table 15-4: bumetanide 0.5–2 mg, torsemide 5–20 mg, furosemide 20–80 mg, ethacrynic acid 50–200 mg.

bank.q: Which loop diuretic has the smallest daily dose (0.5–2 mg)?
bank.why: Bumetanide is the most potent per mg.

bank.q: Which loop diuretic has the largest daily dose (50–200 mg)?
bank.why: Ethacrynic acid 50–200 mg.

bank.q: What is the prototype thiazide diuretic?
bank.why: Slide: prototype drug, hydrochlorothiazide.

bank.q: Thiazide diuretics are used for...
bank.why: Slides: thiazide uses = hypertension, heart failure.

bank.q: Two months after starting a diuretic for hypertension, Ron has a hot, swollen, painful big toe (gout). Which drug?
bank.why: Thiazide toxicity = LUNA: Lipids up, Uric acid up (gout), Na+ down, Allergy.

bank.q: Which is NOT a listed toxicity of thiazide diuretics?
bank.why: Thiazide toxicity: hyperlipidemia, hyponatremia, gout, allergic reactions. Hyperkalemia is the K-sparing diuretics' problem.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a true thiazide but a sulfonamide that acts like one?
bank.why: Thiazide-like (footnote 1): chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone, quinethazone.

bank.q: Which thiazide is given in TWO divided doses?
bank.why: Table 15-6: chlorothiazide (0.5–2 g) and hydroflumethiazide are twice daily; the rest once daily.

bank.q: The daily dose of hydrochlorothiazide in Table 15-6 is...
bank.why: HCTZ 25–100 mg once daily.

bank.q: Potassium-sparing diuretics work by...
bank.a: Preventing K+ secretion by antagonizing aldosterone's effects in the collecting tubules
d: Blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
Blocking NCC in the distal tubule
Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
bank.why: Slide wording. Two groups: aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) and ENaC inhibitors (amiloride, triamterene).

bank.q: A patient has primary hyperaldosteronism with high BP and low K+. Which diuretic fits best?
bank.why: K-sparing uses: hyperaldosteronism, heart failure. Loops and thiazides would lower K+ further.

bank.q: Mr. Domingo, on a diuretic for heart failure, notices tender breast enlargement. Which drug?
bank.why: Spironolactone toxicity: hyperkalemia and gynecomastia (it's a steroid look-alike).

bank.q: Which diuretic can cause HYPERkalemia?
bank.why: K-sparing diuretics (triamterene, amiloride, spironolactone, eplerenone) keep K+ in.

bank.q: Which list follows the nephron in order of the diuretics' sites, from first to last?
bank.why: A-O-L-T-K: All Our Loops Take K+.

bank.q: Which statement correctly compares loop and thiazide diuretics?
bank.a: Loops block NKCC2 in the TAL; thiazides block NCC in the DCT
d: Loops block NCC in the DCT; thiazides block NKCC2 in the TAL
Both block ENaC in the collecting duct
bank.why: Loop = NKCC2/TAL (strongest, for edema); thiazide = NCC/DCT (for hypertension).

bank.q: Loop diuretics act on the distal convoluted tubule.
bank.why: Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb (NKCC2); thiazides act on the DCT.

bank.q: Spironolactone causes hypokalemia.
bank.why: Spironolactone spares K+, so it causes HYPERkalemia.

bank.q: Thiazide diuretics are first-line drugs for hypertension.
bank.why: Thiazides are among the four first-line classes (ACEi, ARB, CCB, thiazide).

bank.q: Which drug is NOT a sympatholytic antihypertensive?
bank.why: Sympatholytics: methyldopa, clonidine, β-blockers, prazosin and α1 blockers, phentolamine/phenoxybenzamine. Hydralazine is a direct vasodilator.
bank.hint: Which one acts directly on the vessel?

bank.q: Sympathetic discharge raises blood pressure through...
bank.a: α1 receptors on vessels (vasoconstriction) and β1 receptors on the heart (↑ rate and force)
d: β2 receptors on vessels and M2 receptors on the heart
bank.why: Slide diagram: α1 → vasoconstriction; β1 → ↑ rate and force (↑ afterload) → ↑ BP.

bank.q: Blocking which receptor lowers BP by reducing heart rate and force?
bank.why: β-blockers block β1 on the heart.

bank.q: Which antihypertensive acts in the brain to lower sympathetic outflow and is the classic choice in pregnancy?
bank.why: Methyldopa (central α2 agonist) = Mom's drug. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.

bank.q: A patient stopped his blood pressure pills suddenly and his BP shot up within a day (rebound hypertension). Which drug is known for this?
bank.why: Textbook extra (not on the slides): abrupt withdrawal of clonidine causes rebound hypertension.

bank.q: Methyldopa and clonidine lower BP by...
bank.a: Stimulating central α2 receptors, so the brain lowers sympathetic outflow
d: Blocking β1 receptors in the heart
bank.why: Both are α2 agonists (Lesson 4).

bank.q: Mang Lito has hypertension and an enlarged prostate. Which drug can help both?
bank.why: α1 blockers (-zosin) relax vessels and the prostate. (Tamsulosin is the most prostate-selective, with the least BP effect.)

bank.q: Which vasodilator is given ORALLY?
bank.why: Oral: hydralazine, minoxidil. Parenteral: nitroprusside, fenoldopam.

bank.q: Which vasodilator is given PARENTERALLY (IV)?
bank.why: Parenteral: nitroprusside, fenoldopam.

bank.q: Which vasodilator works by releasing nitric oxide?
bank.why: Table 11-3: NO release = nitroprusside, hydralazine, nitrates, histamine, acetylcholine. Minoxidil opens K+ channels; fenoldopam hits dopamine receptors; verapamil blocks Ca2+.

bank.q: Which drug lowers BP by opening K+ channels and hyperpolarizing smooth muscle?
bank.why: Hyperpolarization via K+ channels: minoxidil, diazoxide.
bank.hint: Mino and Dia open the K+ door.

bank.q: Diazoxide lowers BP by...
bank.why: Minoxidil and diazoxide = K+ channel openers.

bank.q: Which vasodilator activates dopamine receptors?
bank.why: Fenol-DOPA-m acts on DOPAmine (D1) receptors.

bank.q: Which antihypertensive is sold as a 5% topical solution for hair regrowth?
bank.why: The slide shows topical minoxidil 5% (Regroe): its hair-growth side effect became a hair-regrowth product.

bank.q: Calcium channel blockers lower BP by...
bank.a: Inhibiting Ca2+ influx into arterial smooth muscle cells
bank.why: Slide MOA: inhibition of Ca2+ influx into arterial smooth muscle.

bank.q: Which is a DIHYDROPYRIDINE calcium channel blocker?
bank.why: Dihydropyridines end in -dipine (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine). Verapamil and diltiazem are non-dihydropyridines.

bank.q: A hypertensive patient with a fast heart rate needs a calcium channel blocker that also slows the SA node. Which drug?
bank.why: Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem) also slow the heart; -dipines mainly dilate vessels.
bank.hint: V and D visit the heart.

bank.q: Which calcium channel blocker is NOT a dihydropyridine?
bank.why: Non-DHP: verapamil, diltiazem.

bank.q: Verapamil, diltiazem and nifedipine share which mechanism in Table 11-3?
bank.why: They are the calcium channel blockers.

bank.q: Nitroprusside and fenoldopam are oral vasodilators.
bank.why: Nitroprusside and fenoldopam are parenteral; hydralazine and minoxidil are oral.

bank.q: Minoxidil lowers BP by releasing nitric oxide.
bank.why: Minoxidil opens K+ channels (hyperpolarization); hydralazine and nitroprusside release NO.

bank.q: The renin-angiotensin system is triggered by...
bank.a: A drop in blood pressure or fluid volume
bank.why: Drop in BP or volume → kidney releases renin.

bank.q: Renin is released by the...
bank.why: Renin from the kidney acts on angiotensinogen from the liver.

bank.q: Angiotensinogen is made by the...
bank.why: The liver makes angiotensinogen; renin cuts it to angiotensin I.

bank.q: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) comes mainly from the...
bank.why: ACE (released from the lungs) turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II.
bank.hint: Where blood passes through all at once.

bank.q: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by...
bank.a: Constricting vessels and making the adrenal gland release aldosterone
bank.why: Ang II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone (salt and water retention).

bank.q: Aldosterone acts on the kidneys to...
bank.why: More salt and water kept → more volume → higher BP.

bank.q: Which drug blocks renin?
bank.why: R-A-A-A: Renin (aliskiren) → ACE (-pril) → AT1 receptor (-sartan) → Aldosterone (spironolactone, eplerenone).

bank.q: ACE is the same enzyme as...
bank.why: ACE (kininase II) also breaks down bradykinin. Kallikrein is the enzyme that makes bradykinin from kininogen.

bank.q: Bradykinin lowers blood pressure by...
bank.a: Causing vasodilation and increasing prostaglandin synthesis
bank.why: Bradykinin → vasodilation (+ prostaglandins) → ↓ peripheral resistance.

bank.q: Captopril lowers BP by...
bank.a: Blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to II and the breakdown of bradykinin
bank.why: ACE inhibitors lower Ang II AND raise bradykinin.

bank.q: Which drug is an ACE inhibitor?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors end in -pril: captopril, enalapril, ramipril. Losartan = ARB, aliskiren = renin inhibitor, amlodipine = CCB.

bank.q: Two weeks after starting a new antihypertensive, Lucille has a persistent dry, tickly cough. Which drug is responsible?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors → extra bradykinin → dry cough (and angioedema). ARBs don't affect bradykinin.

bank.q: Which drug gives Lucille the same angiotensin blockade WITHOUT the cough?
bank.why: ARBs block the AT1 receptor and leave bradykinin alone, so no cough.

bank.q: An hour after his new BP pill, a man's lips and face swell up suddenly. Which drug most likely caused it?
bank.why: ACEi toxicity: dry cough, angioedema (the slide's swollen-lip photo), contraindicated in pregnancy.

bank.q: Which antihypertensive is contraindicated in pregnancy?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are contraindicated in pregnancy. Methyldopa and β-blockers can be used.
bank.hint: The E in ACE is for embryo.

bank.q: Elrin has type 2 diabetes, protein in his urine and hypertension. Which drug reduces proteinuria and stabilizes kidney function?
bank.why: Slide: ACE inhibitors are used in chronic kidney disease, especially in diabetics, because they diminish proteinuria.

bank.q: ARBs such as valsartan lower BP by...
bank.why: ARBs block AT1; more selective than ACE inhibitors.

bank.q: Which drug is an angiotensin receptor blocker?
bank.why: ARBs: losartan, valsartan, candesartan, irbesartan, telmisartan.

bank.q: ARBs differ from ACE inhibitors because they...
bank.why: Slide: more selective blockers of angiotensin effects than ACE inhibitors (no effect on bradykinin).

bank.q: Which is NOT an effect of AT1 receptor stimulation?
bank.why: AT1: vasoconstriction, sympathetic activation, cell proliferation, aldosterone release, renal Na+ reabsorption. AT2: vasodilation, inhibition of cell growth, apoptosis.

bank.q: Stimulation of AT2 receptors causes...
bank.a: Vasodilation, inhibition of cell growth and apoptosis
bank.why: ARBs block AT1 and leave AT2 working.

bank.q: On the RAAS diagram, spironolactone and eplerenone block...
bank.why: They act at the end of the cascade (aldosterone → Na+ and water retention).

bank.q: Which lists the RAAS blockers from the TOP of the cascade down?
bank.why: R-A-A-A: Renin, ACE, Angiotensin receptor, Aldosterone.

bank.q: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are both contraindicated in pregnancy.
bank.why: Both block the RAAS, which the fetal kidney needs.

bank.q: Losartan causes a dry cough by raising bradykinin.
bank.why: ARBs have no effect on bradykinin; the cough is an ACE inhibitor problem.

bank.q: In the treatment algorithm, management starts in adults with a BP of...
bank.why: Adults with BP ≥ 140/90 → advise therapeutic lifestyle changes.

bank.q: Which is NOT among the therapeutic lifestyle changes in the algorithm?
bank.why: Lifestyle: low-salt diet, weight loss, exercise, smoking cessation, alcohol abstinence.

bank.q: Mang Pedro has BP 150/95 and had a stroke last year (CV disease). What is the next step?
bank.a: Start a first-line drug along with lifestyle changes
d: Lifestyle changes alone for 3 months first
Refer him to a specialist right away
Start a β-blocker as the only drug
bank.why: With HMOD, CV disease or high risk → choose first-line drugs (monotherapy or combination) right away.

bank.q: Mr. Santos, 40, has BP 145/92 with no organ damage, no CV disease and low risk. What is the next step?
bank.a: Lifestyle changes, then recheck after 3 months
bank.why: Not high risk → lifestyle first; if targets aren't reached after 3 months, start first-line drugs.

bank.q: Which drug is NOT among the first-line choices in the algorithm?
bank.why: First line: ACE inhibitor, ARB, CCB, thiazide (A-C-D). β-blockers wait for a reason.

bank.q: The first-line classes in the algorithm are...
bank.a: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, CCBs and thiazide diuretics
d: β-blockers, α-blockers, loop diuretics and vasodilators
ACE inhibitors, β-blockers, clonidine and minoxidil
Loop diuretics, ARBs, nitroprusside and aliskiren
bank.why: A-C-D: ACEi or ARB, CCB, Diuretic (thiazide).

bank.q: Which is a PREFERRED combination in the algorithm?
bank.why: Preferred: ACEi/ARB + CCB and ACEi/ARB + HCTZ. An ACEi with an ARB doubles up on the same system; two K-sparing drugs risk hyperkalemia.
bank.hint: Mix A with C or D.

bank.q: Which is also a preferred combination?
bank.why: ARB + HCTZ is preferred; the others double up on one class.

bank.q: After 3 months on amlodipine alone, Samantha's BP is still above target. What does the algorithm say?
d: Stop amlodipine and give lifestyle advice only
bank.why: On monotherapy and not at target → add a 2nd agent from the first-line drugs.

bank.q: A patient on two first-line drugs is still above target after 3 months. Next step?
bank.a: Add another drug from the first-line choices
bank.why: Already on 2 drugs → add another first-line drug; if still not at target on the combination → refer.

bank.q: When does the algorithm say to refer the patient?
bank.a: When BP targets aren't reached on the combination drugs
d: After the first month of lifestyle changes
bank.why: Not achieved on combination drugs → refer.

bank.q: Resistant hypertension is BP that stays uncontrolled on...
bank.a: 3 drugs, one of which is a diuretic
bank.why: Footnote: uncontrolled on 3-drug combinations including a diuretic → refer for work-up or second-line agents.

bank.q: In which patient may a β-blocker be the INITIAL antihypertensive?
bank.a: A patient with coronary artery disease
d: A young patient with no other disease
bank.why: β-blockers may be initial therapy with CAD, acute coronary syndrome, high sympathetic drive, or in pregnant women.

bank.q: Which drug is the WRONG choice for a pregnant woman with hypertension?
bank.why: ARBs and ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy. Methyldopa and β-blockers (labetalol) are used.

bank.q: Kyle, hypertensive and diabetic, takes glipizide and an antihypertensive. He is found confused, sweating and trembling. What is the problem, and which drug causes it?
bank.why: Confusion + sweating + trembling = hypoglycemia; glipizide (sulfonylurea) forces insulin release. Name the problem first, then the class.

bank.q: Aleeyah has diabetes with proteinuria and BP 150/95. Which first-line drug also protects her kidneys?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors diminish proteinuria and stabilize renal function, especially in diabetics.

bank.q: A hypertensive man has had repeated gout attacks. Which first-line drug is the poorest choice for him?
bank.why: Thiazides raise uric acid (gout is in their toxicity list).

bank.q: An asthmatic patient needs BP control. Which drug should be AVOIDED?
bank.why: Propranolol is nonselective and blocks β2 in the lungs → bronchospasm.

bank.q: A patient on enalapril is started on another drug and develops a dangerously high K+. Which drug was most likely added?
bank.why: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone (keeping K+) and spironolactone blocks aldosterone: together they raise K+. Loops and thiazides lower K+.

bank.q: A patient took a large overdose of verapamil. Which antidote from Lesson 1 is used?
bank.why: Table 4-9: Ca2+ channel blockers → high-dose insulin and calcium.

bank.q: A patient took a large overdose of his propranolol. Which antidote?
bank.why: Table 4-9: glucagon for β-adrenergic antagonists.

bank.q: Match the ending: a drug ending in -sartan is a(n)...
bank.why: -pril = ACEi, -sartan = ARB, -dipine = CCB, -kiren = renin inhibitor, -olol = β-blocker, -zosin = α1 blocker.

bank.q: A drug ending in -pril is a(n)...
bank.why: -pril = ACE inhibitor (captopril, enalapril, ramipril).

bank.q: A drug ending in -dipine is a(n)...
bank.why: -dipine = DHP CCB (amlodipine, nifedipine…).

bank.q: An ACE inhibitor plus an ARB is one of the preferred combinations.
bank.why: Preferred: ACEi/ARB + CCB, or ACEi/ARB + HCTZ. Combining an ACEi with an ARB doubles up on the same system.

bank.q: According to the algorithm notes, β-blockers may be used as initial therapy in pregnant women.
bank.why: Beta-blockers may be used as initial therapy with CAD, ACS, high sympathetic drive and in pregnant women.

bank.q: Aaliya's repeated readings average 130/79 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 130 is the first stage-1 number (130–139 OR 80–89).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Josh's repeated readings average 120/80 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Trap: 120 looks elevated, but a diastolic of 80 is already in the stage-1 range (80–89), and stage 1 needs only one number.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Yuri's repeated readings average 139/89 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Both numbers are at the top of stage 1 (139 and 89); neither reaches 140 or 90.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Jeorlyn's repeated readings average 140/89 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 140 = stage 2, even though the diastolic is only stage 1. The higher category wins.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Steve's repeated readings average 128/90 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Diastolic 90 alone makes it stage 2 (≥140 OR ≥90).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Sophia's repeated readings average 112/72 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Below 120 AND below 80 = normal.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Harly's repeated readings average 182/100 mmHg. What is the BP category?

bank.q: Christopher's repeated readings average 165/122 mmHg. What is the BP category?

bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Cas's repeated readings average 180/110 mmHg. What is the BP category?

bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Gian's repeated readings average 126/84 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 126 is elevated-range, but diastolic 84 is stage-1 range; stage 1 wins.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Marti's repeated readings average 119/80 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Normal needs a diastolic BELOW 80; 80 is stage 1 (80–89).
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Venice's repeated readings average 135/95 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 135 is stage 1, but diastolic 95 is stage 2; the higher category wins.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Darryl's repeated readings average 124/76 mmHg. What is the BP category?
bank.why: Systolic 120–129 with diastolic below 80 = elevated.
bank.hint: Check BOTH numbers; the higher category wins.

bank.q: Which reading is ELEVATED, not stage 1 hypertension?
bank.why: Elevated = 120–129 AND < 80. 132 is stage-1 systolic; 82 and 80 are stage-1 diastolics.

bank.q: Which reading is hypertension STAGE 2?
bank.why: ≥ 90 diastolic = stage 2 even with a stage-1 systolic.

bank.why: Crisis = ABOVE 180 and/or ABOVE 120. 180/120 is exactly at the limits, so not above.

bank.q: Hypertension stage 1 is defined as...

bank.q: A hypertensive crisis is a BP...
bank.why: Crisis = > 180 and/or > 120.

notes: Safety numbers

Therapeutic index — TD50 ÷ ED50 (higher = safer); slide: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 | Margin of safety — LD1 ÷ ED99 (uses the extremes) | Memory tip — TI uses the middles (50s), margin of safety the edges (1 and 99); bad number on top
4 types of drug toxicity (DAID)

Dose-dependent — worse with concentration and duration | Allergic — hypersensitivity types I–IV | Idiosyncratic — peculiar to one person; primaquine → hemolytic anemia in 10% of black males | Drug-drug interactions — absorption, protein binding, metabolism, receptor, therapeutic action
Dose-dependent examples

Barbiturates — CNS depression (dose-dependent) | Antipsychotics — tardive dyskinesia (duration-dependent) | Tetracyclines — phototoxicity | Acetaminophen — NAPQI → hepatic necrosis (pathological) | Radiation, chemicals, chemo — genotoxic → mutagenic, carcinogenic
Extrapyramidal symptoms (D-P-A-T)

Acute dystonia — hours to 5 days; tongue, neck, face spasm | Parkinsonism — 5–30 days; tremor, shuffling gait | Akathisia — 5–60 days; restlessness | Tardive dyskinesia — months to years; lip-smacking, fly-catching tongue
Hypersensitivity (ACID)
Type I — Anaphylactic: IgE, mast cells, histamine | Type II — Cytolytic (cytotoxic) | Type III — Arthus reaction (immune complex) | Type IV — Delayed (T cells)
Drug-drug interactions

Absorption — ranitidine raises GI pH → more triazolam absorbed | Protein binding — aspirin, barbiturates, phenytoin, sulfonamides, valproic acid, warfarin get displaced | Metabolism — ethanol induces CYP2E1 | Receptor — buprenorphine (partial agonist) blocks narcotic euphoria | Therapeutic action — additive, synergistic, antagonistic
4 kinds of antagonism (F-C-D-R)

Functional — opposite effects via different receptors | Chemical — binds the drug (EDTA chelates Ca and lead) | Dispositional — changes its ADME | Receptor — competitive (surmountable) or noncompetitive
Treating poisoning

Priorities — vital functions; less absorption, more elimination; fight the effects | ABCDE — airway, breathing, circulation, disability (O2, dextrose, naloxone, thiamine), exposure | First step of decontamination — stop the exposure; wash eyes and skin | GI decontamination needs — dangerous poison, still unabsorbed, can be done safely | GI methods — activated charcoal, whole-bowel irrigation, cathartics, gastric lavage, ipecac
Antidotes: metals and alcohols

Dimercaprol (BAL), succimer (DMSA) — lead, mercury, arsenic | EDTA — lead | Penicillamine — lead, mercury, copper | Deferoxamine — iron (de-FE-roxamine) | Fomepizole, ethanol — methanol, ethylene glycol
Antidotes: reverse the drug

Naloxone — opioids | Flumazenil — benzodiazepines | Atropine + pralidoxime (2-PAM) — organophosphates | Physostigmine — anticholinergic syndrome | Glucagon — β-blockers | High-dose insulin, calcium — calcium channel blockers | Digoxin immune Fab — digoxin | Sodium bicarbonate — Na channel blockers
Antidotes: blood and specific drugs

Hydroxocobalamin, thiosulfate — cyanide | Methylene blue — methemoglobinemia | Hyperbaric oxygen — carbon monoxide | Vitamin K1 — warfarin (coumarin) | Leucovorin — methotrexate | Octreotide — sulfonylurea hypoglycemia | N-acetylcysteine — acetaminophen | Pyridoxine (B6) — isoniazid seizures | Dantrolene — malignant hyperthermia | Bromocriptine — neuroleptic malignant syndrome | Benztropine, diphenhydramine — drug-induced dystonia
Phases

Phase 1 — oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; adds a functional group; little more water-soluble; changes activity (often inactivates) | Phase 2 — conjugation; much more water-soluble → excreted | Phase 3 — transport out (ABC transporters) → urine or bile | Memory tip — Phase 1 adds a handle, Phase 2 attaches a big group 2gether
CYP450

What — heme + polypeptide; ~75% of drug metabolism | Reactions — N/O-dealkylation, aromatic hydroxylation, N/S-oxidation, deamination, dehalogenation | Naming — CYP3A4 = family 3, subfamily A, gene 4 | Most active — CYP2C, 2D, 3A | CYP3A4 — metabolizes over 50% of drugs | CYP19 (aromatase) — inhibited by anastrozole
FMOs
Role — minor, benign products, fewer interactions | Most abundant — FMO3 | Substrates — nicotine, cimetidine, ranitidine, clozapine, itopride
CYP inducers (BULLSHIT CRAP GP'S)
Effect — faster metabolism → lower drug levels | List — barbiturates, St. John's Wort, carbamazepine, rifampin, alcohol (chronic), phenytoin, griseofulvin, phenobarbital, sulfonylureas
CYP inhibitors (SICKFACES.COM)

Effect — slower metabolism → higher levels, toxicity | List — sodium valproate, isoniazid, cimetidine, ketoconazole, fluconazole, alcohol (acute binge), chloramphenicol, erythromycin, sulfonamides, ciprofloxacin, omeprazole, metronidazole | Also — grapefruit juice, amiodarone, quinidine | Trap — alcohol is in both: chronic induces, acute binge inhibits
Phase 2 enzymes and their drugs

UGT (glucuronic acid, from UDP-GA) — acetaminophen, morphine, oxazepam, lorazepam | SULT (sulfate, from PAPS) — acetaminophen, steroids, methyldopa | GST (glutathione) — adriamycin, fosfomycin, busulfan | NAT (acetyl) — sulfonamides, isoniazid, dapsone, clonazepam | MT (methyl, from SAM) — L-dopa, methyldopa, mercaptopurine, captopril
Phase 2 details

UGT1A1 — bilirubin; defects in Gilbert, Crigler-Najjar | SULT2A1 — fetal adrenal DHEA-S → placental estrogen | SULT2B1b — skin cholesterol sulfate | Glutathione — glutamic acid + cysteine + glycine | Slow acetylators — isoniazid neuritis, hepatotoxicity; procainamide lupus | TPMT — methylates 6-mercaptopurine (from azathioprine); low TPMT → toxicity
Acetaminophen

~90% — glucuronidation and sulfation (safe) | 5–9% — CYP2E1 → NAPQI (toxic) | Glutathione — neutralizes NAPQI | Overdose — glutathione runs out → hepatic necrosis | Antidote — N-acetylcysteine (refills glutathione) | Ethanol — induces CYP2E1, so drinking worsens it
Sort any autonomic drug
Question 1 — cholinergic or adrenergic system? | Question 2 — mimics or blocks? | Question 3 — direct (receptor) or indirect (enzyme, nerve terminal)?
ANS basics

Sympathetic — fight or flight; thoracolumbar; NE at the organ | Parasympathetic — rest and digest; craniosacral; ACh at the organ | All preganglionic fibers — ACh on Nn | Exception — sympathetic sweat glands use ACh | Adrenal medulla — releases epinephrine into blood | Somatic NMJ — ACh on Nm
Toxidromes

Cholinergic (DUMBBELLS) — Diarrhea/diaphoresis, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm/bronchorrhea, Emesis, Lethargy, Lacrimation, Salivation | Anticholinergic — hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter | Memory tip — cholinergic = wet, anticholinergic = dry and hot
ACh life cycle blockers

Choline uptake (CHT) — hemicholinium | Storage (VAT) — vesamicol | Release (SNAREs) — botulinum toxin | Breakdown (AChE) — the -stigmines and organophosphates (inhibit it) | Memory tip — He Vests Botox, then Stops
Cholinergic receptors
M1 — nerves | M2 — heart (slows it) | M3 — glands, smooth muscle | M4, M5 — CNS | Nm — skeletal muscle NMJ | Nn — ganglia, CNS
Direct muscarinic agonists

Acetylcholine — both receptor types; miotic eye drop | Bethanechol (choline ester) — bladder and bowel retention | Methacholine (choline ester) — bronchial challenge to diagnose asthma | Pilocarpine (alkaloid, M3) — Sjögren, sicca; SE sweating | Muscarinic toxicity — treat with atropine
Direct nicotinic agonists

Nicotine (full), varenicline (partial) — smoking cessation | Succinylcholine (Nm) — depolarizing NMJ blocker | Phase I — depolarization, fasciculations, flaccid paralysis | Phase II — repolarized but desensitized
Indirect (AChE inhibitors) by duration

Short — edrophonium: bedside diagnosis of myasthenia gravis | Intermediate (carbamates, -stigmine) — neostigmine, pyridostigmine: treat myasthenia gravis | Physostigmine — enters the CNS; reverses atropine overdose | Organophosphates (-thion), very long — parathion, malathion: irreversible, pesticides | Nerve gases — tabun, sarin, soman
Alzheimer drugs
Drugs — donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine (AChE inhibitors) | Slide mnemonic — Si Don Pepe, may dementia. Pa Gala Gala sa Riva
Muscarinic blockers

Atropine (prototype, nonselective) — mydriasis; 1st choice for organophosphate poisoning; symptomatic bradycardia; with anesthesia for secretions | Homatropine, cyclopentolate, tropicamide — eye | Ipratropium, tiotropium, umeclidinium, glycopyrronium — asthma, COPD; tiotropium longest | Scopolamine — crosses BBB; motion sickness | Dicyclomine (M3) — diarrhea | Oxybutynin (M3) — urge incontinence | Pirenzepine, telenzepine (M1) — peptic ulcer disease
Nicotinic blockers and regenerators

Hexamethonium — ganglion (Nn) blocker; hypertension (obsolete) | Tubocurarine, pancuronium, atracurium, vecuronium — NMJ (Nm) blockers; muscle relaxation for surgery | Pralidoxime (oxime) — cholinesterase regenerator
Catecholamine life cycle blockers

Synthesis (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting) — metyrosine | Storage (VMAT) — reserpine | Release — guanethidine (blocks); amphetamine, ephedrine, tyramine (cause release) | Reuptake (NET, DAT) — cocaine, tricyclic antidepressants | Memory tip — Met Reserve Guards at Coco's
Adrenergic receptors
α1 — contraction: vessels, sphincters | α2 — relaxation (presynaptic brake) | β1 — one heart: rate, contractility | β2 — two lungs: bronchodilation
Nonselective adrenergic agonists
Norepinephrine — α1 > β1 >>> β2; first line in septic shock | Epinephrine — β1 = β2 > α; anaphylaxis, shock | Dopamine — low D1 (renal), mid β1, high α1; septic shock with renal shutdown
Selective adrenergic agonists

α1 (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline) — decongestants | α2 clonidine — hypertension; off-label ADHD, Tourette | α2 methyldopa — gestational hypertension, preeclampsia | β nonselective isoproterenol — asthma | β1 dobutamine — cardiogenic shock, stress test | β2 salbutamol, terbutaline, isoxsuprine — asthma, tocolysis; SE tremor, tachycardia
Alpha blockers

Phenoxybenzamine — nonselective, irreversible | Phentolamine — nonselective, reversible | Both — pheochromocytoma before surgery (PHE triad: palpitations, headache, excessive sweating) | Prazosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin (α1, -zosin) — BPH; SE orthostatic hypotension; tamsulosin most prostate-selective | Yohimbine (α2) — obsolete; orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction
Beta blockers (-olol)

Nonselective — propranolol, pindolol, timolol, labetalol, carvedilol | Uses — post-MI, hypertension, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, migraine (propranolol) | β1-selective (MANBABE) — metoprolol, atenolol, nebivolol, bisoprolol, acebutolol, betaxolol, esmolol | Esmolol — shortest-acting, IV | LOL trick — A–N β1-selective, O–Z nonselective, not '-olol' (labetalol, carvedilol) = α + β
Pancreatic islets

Alpha (17%) — glucagon | Beta (70%) — insulin | Delta (7%) — somatostatin | F cells — pancreatic polypeptide | Fasting-state hormone — glucagon | Counterregulatory — glucagon, growth hormone, cortisol, epinephrine
Insulin basics

Structure — A and B chains, disulfide bridges; proinsulin has C-peptide | Release — glucose via GLUT2 → ATP → K-ATP channel closes → depolarization → Ca2+ in → exocytosis | Action — GLUT-4 to the membrane; liver stores glycogen, muscle builds protein, fat stores triglyceride
Diabetes types

Type 1 — autoimmune β-cell destruction; absolute deficiency; young; ketoacidosis common; insulin-dependent | Type 2 — insulin resistance + relative deficiency; adults, obese; diet, exercise, oral drugs first; 90–95% of cases | Gestational — pre-eclampsia, macrosomia, caesarean | Metabolic syndrome — 3 of 5: waist, triglycerides ≥150, low HDL, BP ≥130/85, fasting glucose ≥100
Diagnosis and targets

Random glucose — ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms | Fasting glucose — ≥126 mg/dL | 2-h OGTT — ≥200 mg/dL | HbA1c — ≥6.5%; reflects ~3 months | Target HbA1c — <7% (<8% frail elderly) | Pre-meal — 90–130 mg/dL | Postprandial — <180 at 1 h, <150 at 2 h | BP — <140/90 | Type 1 insulin dose — weight (kg) × 0.55 units
Insulins by speed

Rapid (LAG) — lispro, aspart, glulisine: onset 5–15 min, lasts 3–4 h | Short — regular: the one given IV in emergencies, 6–8 h | Intermediate — NPH: peak 6–7 h, 10–20 h | Long (GDD) — glargine ~24 h, detemir 17 h, degludec >42 h; flat, no peak | Main side effect — hypoglycemia
Secretagogues (squeeze out insulin)

Sulfonylureas — close β-cell K+ channels → insulin release | 1st generation — tolbutamide, chlorpropamide, tolazamide (not used) | 2nd generation — glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride, gliclazide | Side effects — hypoglycemia (gliclazide's major SE), weight gain | Meglitinides (-glinide) — repaglinide, mitiglinide: faster, shorter, before meals
Sensitizers (make insulin work)

Metformin (biguanide) — activates AMPK → less liver glucose; first-line T2DM; PCOS | Metformin SE (GLB) — GI upset, lactic acidosis, B12 deficiency | Thiazolidinediones (-glitazone) — pioglitazone, rosiglitazone: PPAR-gamma ligands | TZD SE (FAB-W) — fluid retention/heart failure, anemia, bone fractures, weight gain
Incretin drugs

Incretins (GLP-1, GIP) — boost insulin, block glucagon; DPP-4 breaks them down | GLP-1 agonists (-glutide, exenatide) — exenatide, semaglutide, liraglutide, albiglutide, dulaglutide; weight loss; SE GI upset, pancreatitis | DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptin) — sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, alogliptin, vildagliptin; weight neutral; SE headache, nasopharyngitis, URTI
Excreters and carb blockers

SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozin) — canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin: glucose flows out in urine; SE genital and urinary infections | Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors — acarbose, miglitol: slow carb digestion; lower post-meal spikes only; SE flatulence, diarrhea
Weight effects

Gain — insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, thiazolidinediones | Neutral — alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors | Loss — GLP-1 agonists, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, pramlintide | Memory tip — adding insulin or storing fat adds weight; dumping sugar or curbing appetite removes it
Complications
Microvascular — retinopathy (aneurysms, hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots), nephropathy, neuropathy (foot ulcers) | Macrovascular — stroke, heart attack, peripheral vascular disease
Blood pressure basics

BP — CO × SVR | CO — HR × SV | Systolic — upper number; heart contracting | Diastolic — lower number; heart relaxed | ↑ SVR — viscosity (polycythemia), vessel length (obesity), smaller radius (vasoconstriction)
Hormones and BP (skipped in class)

Raise HR and contractility — norepinephrine, epinephrine | Vasoconstrict — angiotensin II, ADH, NE (α1), epinephrine | Vasodilate — ANP, epinephrine (β2), nitric oxide | Raise volume — aldosterone, ADH | Lower volume — ANP
4 sites of BP control (skipped in class)
Arterioles — resistance | Venules — capacitance | Heart — pump output | Kidneys — volume (renin → angiotensin → aldosterone) | Driver of all four — CNS sympathetic nerves
BP categories

Normal — <120 and <80 | Elevated — 120–129 and <80 | Stage 1 — 130–139 or 80–89 | Stage 2 — ≥140 or ≥90 | Crisis — >180 and/or >120 | Primary (essential) — no specific cause | Secondary — specific etiology
4 classes of antihypertensives
1 — diuretics (deplete body sodium) | 2 — sympathoplegic agents | 3 — direct vasodilators | 4 — block production or action of angiotensin
Diuretic sites (A-O-L-T-K)

PCT — acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) | PCT + descending limb — osmotic (mannitol) | Thick ascending limb — loop (furosemide, torsemide) | DCT — thiazides (HCTZ, chlorthalidone, metolazone) | Collecting duct — K-sparing (spironolactone, triamterene) | Effect — lowers BP 10–15 mmHg; alone for mild–moderate essential hypertension
Loop diuretics

MOA — block NKCC2 (Na/K/2Cl) in the TAL | Prototypes — furosemide, ethacrynic acid | Others — bumetanide, torsemide | Uses — acute pulmonary edema, edema, hyperkalemia, acute renal failure | Toxicity — ototoxicity, allergy | Doses — bumetanide 0.5–2 mg, torsemide 5–20, furosemide 20–80, ethacrynic acid 50–200 | Memory tip — the ear has a loop too
Thiazides

MOA — block NCC (Na/Cl) in the DCT | Prototype — hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) | Uses — hypertension, heart failure | Toxicity (LUNA) — hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia/gout, hyponatremia, allergy | Thiazide-like sulfonamides — chlorthalidone, indapamide, metolazone, quinethazone | Twice daily — chlorothiazide, hydroflumethiazide
Potassium-sparing diuretics

MOA — antagonize aldosterone in the collecting tubules → less K+ secretion | Aldosterone antagonists — spironolactone, eplerenone | ENaC inhibitors — amiloride, triamterene | Uses — hyperaldosteronism, heart failure | Toxicity — hyperkalemia; gynecomastia (spironolactone)
Sympatholytics

Central α2 agonists — methyldopa (pregnancy), clonidine | β-blockers — -olol | α1 blockers — prazosin (-zosin) | Nonselective α blockers — phentolamine, phenoxybenzamine | Why they work — block α1 vasoconstriction and β1 heart rate/force
Direct vasodilators

Oral — hydralazine, minoxidil | Parenteral — nitroprusside, fenoldopam | Release NO — nitroprusside, hydralazine, nitrates | ↓ Ca2+ influx — verapamil, diltiazem, nifedipine | Open K+ channels — minoxidil, diazoxide | Dopamine receptors — fenoldopam | Minoxidil trivia — topical 5% for hair regrowth
Calcium channel blockers

MOA — block Ca2+ influx into arterial smooth muscle | Non-dihydropyridines — verapamil, diltiazem (also slow the SA node) | Dihydropyridines (-dipine) — amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine
RAAS

Trigger — drop in BP or fluid volume | Renin (kidney) — angiotensinogen (liver) → angiotensin I | ACE (lungs) — angiotensin I → angiotensin II | Angiotensin II — vasoconstriction + aldosterone release | Aldosterone — kidneys keep NaCl and water | ACE = kininase II — also breaks down bradykinin (a vasodilator)
Drugs on the RAAS (R-A-A-A)
Renin — aliskiren | ACE — captopril, enalapril, ramipril (-pril) | AT1 receptor — losartan, valsartan, candesartan, irbesartan, telmisartan (-sartan) | Aldosterone — spironolactone, eplerenone
ACE inhibitors vs ARBs

ACEi MOA — block Ang I → Ang II and bradykinin breakdown | ACEi in CKD — less proteinuria, stable renal function (diabetics) | ACEi toxicity — dry cough, angioedema, not in pregnancy | ARB MOA — block AT1; no bradykinin effect | ARB advantage — no cough; switch to it after an ACEi cough | AT1 — vasoconstriction, sympathetic activation, cell growth, aldosterone, Na reabsorption | AT2 — vasodilation, less cell growth, apoptosis
Treatment algorithm

Start — BP ≥140/90 → lifestyle: low salt, weight loss, exercise, no smoking, no alcohol | High risk (HMOD, CV disease) — start drugs now | Not high risk — 3 months of lifestyle first | First line — ACEi, ARB, CCB, thiazide (A-C-D) | Not at target after 3 months — add a 2nd, then a 3rd first-line drug; then refer | Preferred combos — ACEi/ARB + CCB, ACEi/ARB + HCTZ | β-blockers first — CAD, ACS, high sympathetic drive, pregnancy | Resistant hypertension — uncontrolled on 3 drugs incl. a diuretic → specialist
